pass1.reasoningLog:
**What I am claiming, and how strong it is**

I am reading DISPLACEMENT, early-stage and only moderately supported. This is a positive-deterioration claim, not an absence-of-deterioration claim: prime-age employment is falling (12-month change -0.5, as of 2026-06), the long-term unemployed share is up 4.0 points over twelve months to 27.3% (2026-06), and this is happening while the exposed-industry divergence sits past its attribution alarm line. But I want to be explicit about how thin the reabsorption half is. Prime-age employment is still 0.25 points *above* its 2019 reference level, hires-minus-quits improved over the last year, and the underemployment gap widened by only 0.1 point. The deterioration I am leaning on is recent, small in absolute terms, and concentrated in one quarter. A reasonable analyst looking at the same payload could call this reallocation and would not be being unreasonable. I am picking displacement because the attribution is unambiguous, the controls are healthy, the absorption channel is bending in the wrong direction on two of four readouts, and — most importantly — the one panel that could have shown exposed workers being made *more valuable* is disqualified by its own weighting rule.

**Panel by panel**

*exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-06, 1 month old) — ATTRIBUTION.* Name the sides: exposed industries (information, professional/business services, finance) are at **-1.3% year-over-year job growth**; control industries (construction, leisure/hospitality, education/health) are at **+1.3%**. The differential is -2.5, exactly at the registered trigger, and 2.08 SD past normal against the fixed 2010-01 to 2019-12 window — over the alarm line of 2. Against full history it is only 0.75 SD, and I am reasoning from the pre-2020 figure as instructed, because full history has swallowed 2023-onward into its definition of normal (its mean differential is -1.58 versus -0.99 pre-2020, and its low of -5.22 is dated 2023-11, i.e. inside the period under test). The prior reading was -2.61, so the gap is fractionally *narrower* than last month — the divergence is holding, not accelerating. Two consecutive months past the alarm line, described as roughly flat.

This panel establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work. It does not establish that work was destroyed, and the mechanics in its own artifact block are decisive on that point: if 100 jobs moved from information to construction, exposed falls, control rises, the gap widens from both ends, and nobody is displaced. Control employment growing at +1.3% is exactly the destination such a flow would have. I also do not attribute precision to the industry proxy — a janitor in the information sector counts as exposed, a data analyst in manufacturing does not.

*reabsorption (headline as_of 2026-06; JOLTS components 2026-05) — REABSORPTION.* The headline is the prime-age employment-population ratio at 80.2%, 12-month change **-0.5, falling**, scored at 1.77 SD toward displacement against the fixed pre-2020 window (attention line 1, alarm line 2). Both baselines agree here (divergence 0.03), so this does not depend on the window choice. One instrument inconsistency I want on the record: the panel reports the pre-2020 mean 12-month change as -0.42 with SD 0.52, and -0.5 is only about 0.15 SD below that mean, which does not reconcile with a reported deviation of 1.77. I cannot resolve that from what I have. The panel's own threshold rule is "deterioration is the headline's 12-month change reaching 1 SD below its 2010-01 to 2019-12 norm," and by the reported deviation field that rule is met; by the raw mean and SD it is not. I am treating the reported deviation as the dashboard's scoring and flagging that a reader who recomputes from the baseline moments will get a milder answer. This weakens my confidence and is part of why I call the verdict moderate rather than strong.

The fast horizon is context only and I am not voting it, but it is the most interesting number on the panel: the 3-month change is **also -0.5**. Mechanically, that means prime-age employment was roughly flat for nine months and then gave up half a point in a single quarter. Its 3-month deviation is 2.85 against the fixed window, past the alarm line. That is a hypothesis about a fresh turn, not a finding, and 3-month moves on a household survey are noisy. But the two horizons agree in direction, and the concentration of the decline is why I do not read the still-healthy *level* as reassurance — the panel itself warns that a level scored against a fixed 2019 reference is slow to register a fresh turn from a high starting point. That is precisely the situation.

Secondary readouts, none of which vote:
- Long-term unemployed share **27.3%, +4.0 points over 12 months, rising**. Deviation 0.96, just under the attention line; the 3-month change is +1.9 at 1.46 SD. The 12-month change SD on this series is 5.2, so +4 points is inside one standard deviation of its own history. Direction is clearly adverse; magnitude is not yet abnormal. Read as: exits are taking longer to land.
- Hires minus quits **1.4 rate points, +0.1 over 12 months, rising** (as_of 2026-05, one month older than the headline). Deviation -0.9, i.e. away from displacement. Name the moving side: hires 3.3, quits 1.9. This is a low-churn market on both legs — the net looks fine partly because voluntary quitting is subdued, not because hiring is strong. A low-hire market and a rising long-term unemployed share are the same fact seen twice: anyone who leaves waits longer. This readout is the strongest single thing arguing against my verdict.
- U-6 minus U-3 **3.7 points, +0.1 over 12 months, rising**, deviation 1.48 against the fixed window (0.90 against full history; preferring the clean window). 3-month change flat, disagreeing with the 12-month direction. Mild widening — people landing slightly worse, not dramatically so.

*Contemporaneous macro test.* The yield curve is not inverted (10y-2y +0.4, as_of 2026-07) and I am not using it to exculpate anything — it prices the future, not the weakness already in the June data. The correct test is whether the controls are weak, and they are not: control employment +1.3% y/y (2026-06), control postings 3.9% *above* their own February 2020 level (2026-07), control pay +3.5% (2026-06). A general macro slump that produced -1.3% in information/professional/finance should be visible in construction, leisure and health, and it is not. This test cuts *for* my verdict, and I would have reported it against had it come out the other way.

*exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-06).* Exposed pay +4.6% y/y, control +3.5%, differential +1.1, which is above the pre-2020 mean of 0.7 and 0.82 SD *away* from displacement; 23 months inside its own 2010s range. On its face this is the augmentation panel. The weighting rule disqualifies it: exposed employment y/y is -1.27%, falling, and when a group is shrinking the average wage rises mechanically as lower-paid workers exit, with nobody getting a raise. The control side compounds it — leisure and hospitality is low-wage and growing, dragging the control average down. So this panel cannot distinguish augmentation from displacement and I am not citing it as support for either. I want to be plain that my verdict runs *against* the direction of this panel and that I am setting it aside on a stated measurement rule rather than because it points my way.

*job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-07, freshest panel).* Sides first: exposed knowledge-work postings at **76.3, i.e. 23.7% below their own February 2020 level**; control hands-on postings at **103.9, 3.9% above theirs**. Spread -28. No pre-2020 baseline exists (series begins 2020-02), so this is a level-and-direction read only. Direction cuts against me: the spread has *improved* 3 points over 6 months, sits 1.35 SD better than its own 2023-onward mean of -33.35, and is well off its 2023-10 low of -42.7. Postings lead hiring, and the leading indicator is healing, not deteriorating. That is a genuine problem for the displacement reading and it is the freshest panel on the board.

*labor_productivity (as_of 2026-03, 4 months old).* 2.8% y/y, up from 2.5%, first quarter inside the 2.7-3.4 "internet-boom" band; the registered break is above 3.4 for two straight quarters, which has not happened. About 1.4 SD above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27. Note the vintage gap: this is a quarter-plus older than the June/July labor panels, so it cannot reflect any recent turn. Output per hour accelerating while exposed employment shrinks is the arithmetic signature of the same work being done with fewer hours. It is also the arithmetic signature of augmentation. It does not discriminate on its own.

*worker_share_of_income (as_of 2026-03, 4 months old).* 51.0% of gross domestic income — the low of the entire 1947-onward history. Four consecutive quarterly declines; -1.0 over four quarters, against a 40-year drift of -0.13 per year and a 10-year drift of -0.20 per year, so roughly seven times the secular pace, and in the fastest decile of all 4-quarter changes on record. This panel is **economy-wide** and by explicit registration has no threshold, because recessions produced faster falls (-2.18 in 2009-12, -1.59 in 2010-03) and any trigger set here would fire on recessions. I cannot use it as evidence about exposed industries and I am not doing so. What I take from it: the 2.8% productivity acceleration is not showing up in labor's share, and it is happening without a recession (unemployment 4.2%, payrolls +57k, controls growing). That is context, not proof, and it is context about all workers, not exposed ones.

*recent_grad_gap (as_of 2026-06).* 2.6 points, above its trailing 10-year average, 150-month streak of graduates faring worse. Supplemental by registration. The streak length is the caveat: graduates have *always* been above the general rate, so only the position above trailing average carries any signal, and that trailing average includes the test period. Directionally consistent with entry-level knowledge work being squeezed; carries almost no weight.

*ai_adoption (as_of 2026-07).* 21.7% of firms, up from 17.3% in 2025-11, seven of nine collections higher. Large firms (250+) at 38.8% versus 20.8% for 1-4 employees, gradient 1.87, so worker exposure exceeds the firm-count share — I am not stating a worker-weighted number because none is measured. This is a weak-form deployment gate: it permits a displacement reading and causes nothing. Gate satisfied.

*ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation (as_of 2025-09, 10 months old, stale).* 43.1% automation / 56.9% augmentation, essentially unchanged across the three releases that exist. Per its own staleness warning I give this no weight in a current call beyond noting stability. It predates every labor panel here by most of a year and cannot describe how AI is being used in mid-2026. It is worth flagging that this is a counterweight to my verdict and it is the oldest thing on the dashboard — it cannot reflect a recent turn in usage mix.

*Capability panels (METR 2026-04; GDPval-AA Elo 2026-07; GDPval-vs-experts 2025-12, stale; benchmark tracks 2026-07).* Descriptive only, vote on nothing, and I am treating them that way. Noted: the GDPval human-comparison series is 7 months old and its 70.9% figure is wins-plus-ties, self-reported by the lab, with true wins-only parity at 49.7%. None of this moves the reading.

**The 2021-22 hiring correction, weighed against me**

Information, professional/business services and finance over-hired in 2021-22 and have been unwinding since. This is available as a full non-AI account and it explains a lot: it explains the 2023-11 trough of -5.22 on the jobs differential (deepest point of the unwind), it explains why exposed postings have been below their February 2020 level continuously since the series' 2023 window opens, and it plausibly explains a good part of why exposed postings are still at 76.3 today. It also explains the low-churn market — a sector that overhired stops hiring and its workers stop quitting.

What it explains less well: a hiring correction is a level adjustment, and four to five years in you would expect it to have run its course, with exposed employment flattening at a lower level rather than still printing -1.3% year-over-year in 2026-06. The postings recovery is consistent with the correction ending; the continued outright employment decline is not obviously consistent with it. That is the residual: an exposed sector still shedding jobs after the correction's own leading indicator has turned up, alongside productivity in the internet-boom band and labor's share at a 79-year low. I do not think the correction can carry all of that, but I concede it carries more than half, and that is why this is a moderate call.

**Inversions — every panel I lean on, read the other way**

1. *Exposed-vs-control jobs (-1.3 / +1.3).* Strongest opposite reading: this is the fingerprint of successful reallocation, and the panel says so itself — perfect reallocation with every worker re-employed produces the maximally negative reading. Control industries are adding jobs at +1.3% and their postings are above pre-pandemic. If AI is compressing headcount in information and professional services and those workers are being absorbed into health care and construction, this panel looks identical to what I am calling displacement while nobody is displaced. Control industries adding jobs at 1.3% is precisely the destination such a flow would need. And a market with little hiring and little quitting lengthens spells for everyone regardless of cause.

2. *Frozen hiring market from the rate cycle.* This is the strongest competing cause and the layoffs readout (1.1, flat, deviation 0.38) plus the postings artifact block (spread opened in 2022, attributed substantially to rates) support it. (iii) Every panel that moved since the last run moved trivially (-0.04, +0.01, +0.9, 0.0). This is a quiet month. The verdict rests on levels that were already there, not on new movement, and I would rather say that plainly than dress a flat month as a development.

Jobs in exposed versus control industries. Naming both sides rather than the gap: the exposed side is in outright contraction, down 1.27% year over year, and the control side is growing at 1.27%. That combination is what rules out a general downturn. If this were the ordinary business cycle, construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health would be weak too, and they are not — they are the ones adding jobs. Interest rates are not signalling recession either, though I am not leaning on that in either direction; a signal that says "no recession" cannot explain away weakness that is visibly there. What the control-industry strength buys me is specificity: whatever is hitting information and professional services is not hitting the whole economy. The strongest argument against the exposed-jobs finding is the hiring correction. Information and professional and business services hired far too aggressively in 2021 and 2022 and have been letting that unwind ever since. The postings data carries its own note saying the exposed-versus-control gap in job advertisements opened in 2022 and attributes a substantial part of it to the interest-rate cycle rather than to anything models did. That explains the opening of both gaps, and probably a fair part of why exposed employment is still below where its old trend would have put it in 2026. What it does not explain is why the gap is still here. An unwind decays. Four years on, the exposed side is not merely below trend, it is contracting year over year, while the controls — which also overhired, in leisure and hospitality — are growing. That leftover is what I am reading. It is a smaller thing than the raw two-and-a-half-point gap suggests, and I want that said rather than buried.

Closing is what recovery, or genuine augmentation, would look like. Absorption. The level of prime-age employment is not alarming — 80.2% of 25-to-54-year-olds have a job, which is fractionally above where it stood in 2019. The direction is what is bad. Hiring is weak at 3.3% and quits at 1.9%, and the gap between them has actually improved slightly over the year. Weak hiring plus normal layoffs is not an economy shedding workers, it is an economy that has stopped taking people in. That is a frozen market, and a frozen market has a perfectly good non-AI explanation in interest rates and business uncertainty. It also puts most of the burden on people trying to enter work, who are mostly under 25 and therefore mostly outside the 25-to-54 group the headline employment rate covers. Mixed evidence is not the same as an identified alternative cause.

There is a specific reason to distrust it here: if entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped, the workforce that remains skews more senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. The economy-wide individual-level trackers sit at 3.6% for people who stay in their jobs and 4.4% for people who move — both well below 4.63% — which hints that the exposed-industry figure is partly composition. I cannot prove it, because those trackers cover the whole economy and cannot be cut to exposed industries. So the composition question stays open and the panel stays weak, in both directions.

The new panel: individual wage growth. This follows the same people over time, which is what makes it useful as a check on the composition problem above. People who change jobs are still earning about eight-tenths of a point more growth than people who stay, a premium above its pre-2020 average of about six-tenths, and it has been recovering over recent readings. That is the shape of people moving because they see something better, not because they were pushed. It is the cleanest single argument against the displacement reading, and unlike the productivity and labour-share numbers it cannot be dismissed as covering the wrong workers — it covers everyone, exposed workers included. Two things temper it without disposing of it. It is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority is precisely the shape it would miss. And the household survey behind it has been degrading, with October 2025 missing outright.

Productivity. Output per hour is growing at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, which sits at the low edge of the late-1990s internet-boom range for one quarter. Real aggregate gains showing up is what augmentation working looks like, and I take it seriously. Two things stop it from overturning the reading. It is economy-wide, so none of it can be attributed to AI-exposed work specifically. And output per hour is a ratio: it rises mechanically when hours are cut faster than output falls, so a firm producing the same with fewer people generates exactly this number. Rising productivity sitting on top of falling prime-age employment does not tell augmentation and displacement apart. This figure is also four months old, from the first quarter, against labour data running to June and July — a real gap, and worth flagging because this panel is the load-bearing piece of the augmentation counter-case.

Labour share of income. The share of national income going to workers rather than to capital has fallen to 51.0%, a new low for the full history, with four consecutive quarterly declines and a one-point fall over four quarters — a pace in the fastest tenth on record and many times the slow drift of the past forty years. Directionally this fits the displacement reading. I give it no weight in the verdict: it is economy-wide, it has no threshold, and on the historical record a measure like this fires in recessions, not on technology.

AI adoption. 21.7% of firms report using AI in some business function, up from 17.3% in November 2025, with large employers at 38.8% — so the share of workers in an AI-using firm is well above the share of firms. This establishes that AI use is now widespread enough that a labour effect is possible. It causes nothing and I am not treating its rise as evidence that anything has happened to workers.

Capability benchmarks. Read and counted in nothing. The leading model can now sustain tasks of a few hours' length at the measured reliability threshold, and on one professional-task benchmark models reached about 71% wins-plus-ties in December 2025 — though wins alone were just under half, and that is a lab reporting on its own benchmark with nothing published since. None of this is an event in anyone's employment.

Two alternatives I considered and rejected as the named cause. First, shrinking labour supply from immigration enforcement. If the prime-age population is genuinely falling, employment can fall with nobody being displaced. I reject it because the population series has been disqualified by its own documentation, as above, and because immigration-sensitive employment concentrates in construction and leisure and hospitality — the control industries, which are growing. A supply shock that spares the control side and hits information and professional services is the wrong shape. Second, the frozen hiring market, discussed above.

Two cross-panel oddities worth recording. The household survey says prime-age employment is down 1.38% over the year while the establishment survey says payrolls grew by 57,000 in the latest month and control industries grew 1.27% over the year. These are different surveys covering different things and it is wrong to net them against each other, but a disagreement that large is a reason to hold the household-based absorption reading loosely, particularly given the documented decline in household survey response rates. Separately, the headline employment rate's level says the market is fine and its change says it is deteriorating; that is expected, and the right way to read it is level for where we are, change for which way we are going. Overall the news picture is soft but positive: 57,000 jobs added, unemployment at 4.2%. A labour market destroying work wholesale does not usually add payrolls. That sits comfortably with the frozen-market story and uncomfortably with mine.

What would show the displacement reading is wrong. Absorption returning. Specifically: the prime-age employment rate climbing back so its twelve-month change is no worse than a tenth of a point down, while the long-term unemployed share falls back to 26% or below, by late October. The first says people are landing again; the second guards against a bounce that leaves the people already stranded still stranded. Both are reachable — the employment rate moved half a point in a single quarter, and the long-term share moved nearly two points in three months — and both publish monthly, so three more readings land before the deadline. I deliberately did not make the second test "the exposed-versus-control jobs gap closes." At its recent pace of movement it could not get to a meaningful level by October, and a test that cannot fire is worthless. It is also the wrong test: if people start landing while the industry gap stays open, that is reallocation with a functioning labour market, and reallocation is exactly the finding that would make a displacement reading wrong.

PUBLISHED_NOTE:
The reading is displacement, and it rests on something happening rather than on the absence of good news: jobs in AI-exposed industries are actually shrinking, by 1.27% over the past year, while jobs in the control industries AI has barely touched grew 1.27%, and the people coming out are not landing again.

Nothing moved this month. The jobs gap between exposed and control industries shifted by four hundredths of a point, pay growth on each side by a hundredth, the share of firms using AI not at all. The household and payroll figures still run through June, so every labour reading is the one from last month. The reading rests on levels that were already there, not on fresh deterioration, and that is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up a flat month.

The one new thing is a measure that follows the same individuals over time, and it argues against displacement — see below.

What makes this displacement rather than workers reshuffling between industries is the absorption side. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job has fallen half a percentage point over twelve months, in a series that normally rises about four-tenths of a point a year, and prime-age employment itself is down about 1.4 million people, so this is not an artefact of a growing population. The share of unemployed people out of work six months or longer has climbed four points to 27.3%. If only the exposed industries were weak, that would be reallocation. People staying unemployed longer is what turns it into displacement.

Three things cut the other way and one of them is new.

Postings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs — but that gap has been closing, by 3.9 points over six months and nine-tenths in the last month. Closing is what recovery looks like. This is the freshest data on the board, a month ahead of everything supporting the displacement reading, and it points the other way. One caveat readers deserve: the published figures show the change in the gap but not in each side separately, so it is impossible to tell whether knowledge-work postings are recovering or hands-on postings are falling back. If it is the second, the narrowing is not good news at all.

The new individual-level pay data shows people who change jobs still getting about eight-tenths of a point more wage growth than people who stay, above the pre-2020 norm of six-tenths and recovering. That is people moving because they see something better, not because they were pushed. It covers the whole workforce, including exposed workers, so it cannot be waved away as measuring the wrong people. It is a median, though, so a collapse concentrated in a minority is exactly what it would miss.

And layoffs are entirely normal, at 1.1% of employment, while hiring is weak. That combination is not an economy shedding workers, it is one that has stopped taking people in. A frozen market has a perfectly good explanation in interest rates, and its burden falls mainly on people entering work, who are mostly under 25 and mostly outside the prime-age figures above.

There is also a real residual to be honest about. Information and professional services overhired badly in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding since, and that explains why these gaps opened. It does not explain why they are still here. An unwind decays; four years on, exposed employment is not just below trend but contracting outright, while the controls — which also overhired, in leisure and hospitality — are growing. That leftover is what this reading is built on, and it is a thinner thing than the headline gap suggests.

Two figures that get quoted as evidence do not belong here. Productivity growth at 2.8% a year and the worker share of national income at a record-low 51.0% both cover the whole economy, not AI-exposed work, and output per hour rises mechanically whenever hours are cut faster than output falls. Neither tells augmentation and displacement apart.

What to watch: the prime-age employment rate in the reabsorption panel. If it turns back up, people are landing again and this reading is wrong.
